title: interdisciplinarity within and beyond geography: introduction to special section
display_name: Interdisciplinarity within and beyond geography: introduction to Special Section
abstract: this special section presents a selection of papers given at the institute of british geographers conference held in 2007 in a session titled interdisciplinarity within and beyond geography . there is a long debate on working across disciplinary perspectives within geography, taken up since 2003 in the conversations across the divide sessions at the rgs-ibg conferences. conversations across the divide have developed into activity across the divide , for example, in the british-based rural economy and land use (relu) programme, in which every project supported had to be interdisciplinary across the social and natural sciences. the aim of the conference session was, first, to reflect on practices across the divide within, and beyond, geography. secondly, it aimed to examine where these theoretical and empirically based activities are taking us. five of the oral presentations have been developed into papers presented in this special section, four were from research conducted within relu-funded programmes. we talk here about interdisciplinarity as a practice associated with the development of systematic analyses bringing together the natural and social world. it is a practice that brings to the fore the emergent properties of complex systems and the need for methodological pluralism as a way to understand multiply determined situations in the world. the papers in this special section explore aspects of interdisciplinary practices more closely. we argue that the need for justifying interdisciplinary research seems to have passed and the benefits of, and problems associated with doing, interdisciplinary research are widely recognised.1 existing literatures cover definitions of interdisciplinarity, reflections on experiences of interdisciplinary projects, reasons for undertaking interdisciplinary research and on championing certain subjects as examples of best practice. two aspects of interdisciplinary working stand out as needing further work in the future. first, some attention has been given to those cultural and social circumstances that make interdisciplinary research difficult. the papers in this special section go some way towards understanding these effects, working through cultures of practice, but nevertheless deeper understandings of the processes involved still need to be explored. second, earlier criticisms of interdisciplinarity suggested that research of this type lacked the theoretical and methodological foundations that disciplines take for granted. and as a consequence, the criteria for judgement what is or is not good interdisciplinary knowledge is still underdeveloped. as the evidence accumulates, it is becoming clear that the quality of interdisciplinary research in general is being tested in a similar manner to disciplinary research; by rigour, good practice and peer assessment. however, standard practices, particularly in the more positivist sciences, tend to use replicability as a measure of validation. in interdisciplinary research projects it becomes more difficult to argue for the same approach. one of the ways in which interdisciplinary work can be more widely tested is through comparative studies across networks of research and practice. and there is room for more critical self reflection through comparative work at different scales. this collection of papers starts to identify key details of the practices involved in successful integrative work. four papers in this special section look particularly at the ways in which interdisciplinarity is performed in this role: harris et al. (pp ** **) provide an overview of ten teams looking at research motivations; oughton and bracken (pp ** **) examine the ways in which the external and internal environments of research affect the framing of an interdisciplinary research project; buller and wesselink (pp ** **, ** **) focus upon the role and use of boundary objects. in their paper harris et al. concentrate on the motivations of people doing interdisciplinary research, the process of the research teams coming together and the relationships that were built up during the work. the ten teams examined are composed of academics from different disciplines, representatives from commercial agricultural-based businesses and scientists working in the third sector. the paper highlights that in six out of the ten case studies funding bodies had determined the need for interdisciplinary research. specific challenges that interviewees raised included the high emotions that emerged during negotiation of project aims, the difficulties in terms of career progression of doing interdisciplinary research, problems of deciding how, when and where to publish results, debates concerning methodologies to be employed, and finally, how to build trust between researchers involved in such projects. oughton and bracken, using projects that look at a wider range of landscape issues, investigate the framing of interdisciplinary research by analysing 15 semi-structured interviews with the academics leading these projects. framing was found to be complex, influenced by factors both exogenous and endogenous to the process, especially the negotiation between researchers from different disciplines, and involved finding different ways of being interdisciplinary. one key factor that oughton and bracken highlight is the continued re-framing that takes place during the lifetime of the research, not just the initial framing at the outset of a project. their paper highlights the fuzziness and dynamic nature of the research boundary and the stimulus that this provides for negotiation. buller, drawing from a backdrop of food chain research, considers the practice and performance of interdisciplinarity as a lively process of knowledge creation that operates within forums of articulation through which epistemologically mobile socio-natural entities are defined and explored. he notes the importance of boundary objects or relata , which were used as the agents of interdisciplinarity, circulating in different forms and commanding different understandings. buller proposes that discussion of these key materials acts as fora for the articulation of different knowledges. important points in the process of interdisciplinarity are the identification of objects for discussion and how these are bounded by different disciplines, how the objects are translated during on-going discussions, and then how the quality of an object to the research is mediated. wesselink develops similar ideas to buller by exploring the new knowledge produced by both inter- and transdisciplinary research. initially wesselink explores the types of knowledge produced by different classifications of interdisciplinary research. she then teases out how knowledge produced by interdisciplinary research may be different from that produced by disciplinary research by examining her own study on the meuse flood management study. wesselink concludes that interdisciplinary knowledge production implies the need for integration of facts and values into a new emergent property or synthesis. this is not necessarily different from disciplinary research, but because there is no prevalent set of values in interdisciplinary knowledge production, it is much more important to negotiate boundary objects. in a similar vein to buller, wesselink sees these boundary objects as the starting point for interdisciplinary collaboration. the final paper in this collection, by white et al., (pp ** **) changes direction to focus on examining the effectiveness of policy-relevant interdisciplinary research. an important measure of the quality of interdisciplinary practice is developing/having the opportunity to compare work in different sites, exploring the relative success of projects and identifying what we can learn from the comparison. the paper is based on a questionnaire survey of international integrative (inter- and transdisciplinary) projects focused on environmental issues in rural areas and personal reflections from the team's own research. white et al. highlight several factors for success of integrative projects: the need for a clear conceptual framework, use of appropriate scales, effective language and communication, time and commitment, and trust and respect. an enhanced opportunity to engage with policymakers and stakeholders at all stages of the research was seen to bring improved understandings of the context of research and how it can be applied to inform policy. at the same time this can help to frame new policy-relevant research questions. interdisciplinary ways of working have become much more widely accepted practices over the past five years and recognised as fundamental to dealing with many of the large issues facing society in the early twenty-first century. these ways of working have unsettled habits of scientific practice; aspects of this unsettling have been explored in the papers here and in the wider literature reflecting on interdisciplinarity. we suggest that we've now reached the point where further research should focus on critical reflection linked more firmly with theoretical understandings of interdisciplinarity.

title: toward an integrative science of life-span development and aging
display_name: Toward an Integrative Science of Life-Span Development and Aging
abstract: the study of aging demands an integrative life-span developmental framework, involving interdisciplinary collaborations and multiple methodological approaches for understanding how and why individuals change, in both normative and idiosyncratic ways. we highlight and summarize some of the issues encountered when conducting integrative research for understanding aging-related change, including, the integration of results across different levels of analysis; the integration of theory, design, and analysis; and the synthesis of results across studies of aging. we emphasize the necessity of longitudinal designs for understanding development and aging and discuss methodological issues that should be considered for achieving reproducible research on within-person processes. it will be important that current and future studies permit opportunities for quantitative comparison across populations given the extent to which historical shifts and cultural differences influence life-span processes and aging-related outcomes.

title: virtual reality and museum tourism in the anchoring paradigm
display_name: Virtual reality and museum tourism in the anchoring paradigm

authorships.name: Jiang Gu
institutions: Nanjing University of Finance and Economics

abstract: the present research designed a series of two studies and examined the impacts of the additional vr tour on museum tourist behaviour, learning and satisfaction, considering tourists' belief of technology in the anchoring paradigm. it finds that museum tourists with an additional vr tour of cultural exhibitions spend less time and show a targeted temporal spatial pattern in the on-site visit than those without vr. the findings indicated that participants who read the poster about vr are advanced and helpful in museum visits and reported higher learning and satisfaction compared with those who did not read the poster, no matter whether they took the additional vr tour or not. this finding suggests that external anchors significantly influence and even bias people's judgements in visitor learning and satisfaction with their visit to cultural exhibitions. this study is among the first to look into the human-technology relationship, particularly the sentiment of 'technological optimism' in the tourism context. using the anchoring theory, this study investigates museum tourists' cognitive mechanism involving their belief in technology. it is also innovative in employing interdisciplinary methods, such as spatial-temporal analysis, in-depth interviews, observations and experiments.

title: history and critical marketing studies
display_name: History and critical marketing studies
abstract: purpose the purpose of this paper is to argue that the function of history in critical marketing studies centres on the issue of contextualisation. it aims to put forward the idea that historically informed critical marketing studies highlight that key institutions, actors and scholarly writings have all helped to constitute, perform and destabilise marketing theory, thought and practice in ways that reflect multiple constellations of interests. design/methodology/approach by way of an engagement with various strands of the literature, it is suggested that the history of marketing thought and marketing history are riven with power relations. they include economically derived power relations and culturally significant changes in the social environment. however, while important, they are only part of a more pluralistic tapestry of factors that come from sometimes completely unrelated areas that helped constitute the conditions which fostered a given area of inquiry, debate and so on, in marketing and consumer research. findings weaved into accounts such as those articulated within critical marketing studies are attempts to rethink aspects of theory, concept formation, thought, practice and institutions that have assumed a taken for granted status. originality/value this account is based on a detailed reading of interdisciplinary debates read into the history of marketing thought and marketing history.

title: a cross-cultural comparison of chinese and western philosophical practice: exploring new paths for philosophical healing and social harmony
display_name: A cross-cultural comparison of Chinese and Western philosophical practice: exploring new paths for philosophical healing and social harmony
abstract: abstract philosophical practice applies philosophical insights and methods to help individuals explore and resolve intellectual, emotional, and existential dilemmas, enhancing self-understanding and mental well-being. this study employs citespace to analyze global research trends and hotspots in philosophical practice using data from the web of science (wos) and china national knowledge infrastructure (cnki) databases spanning from 2000 to 2024. by identifying key methodologies and applications, the study compares the development of philosophical practice in western and chinese contexts across theoretical culture, practical application, social impact, and professional development. the findings reveal that western philosophical practice, rooted in ancient greek philosophy and modern streams like existentialism and analytic philosophy, emphasizes individual autonomy, critical thinking, and personal growth. in contrast, chinese philosophical practice draws from confucianism, daoism, and buddhism, focusing on harmony between the individual and society, moral cultivation, and social cohesion. despite these differences, both traditions share common goals of enhancing self-awareness, addressing ethical dilemmas, and improving mental health through philosophical dialogue. the study highlights the potential for integrating chinese and western philosophical practice, suggesting that a fusion of methodologies and ethical frameworks can provide a more holistic and culturally sensitive approach. this integration offers new perspectives for global philosophical dialogue, interdisciplinary collaboration, and practical applications in addressing contemporary challenges.
